strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: personalizing frozen VLAs to manipulate user-specific objects among visually similar distractors is a practically important gap that current VLA benchmarks do not test, and the paper articulates the 'control gap' relative to prior personalization work (VLAS, PIN, MEMENTO) convincingly.

The proposed VAP method is simple, training-free, and deployable: reference images form a non-parametric memory, grounding is done with open-vocabulary detection + embedding voting across reference views, and the mask is injected via a semi-transparent highlight plus a template-based instruction rewrite. No VLA parameters change, so new objects are usable immediately after registration.

Comprehensive evaluation across two newly constructed simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench) and a real-world SO-101 setup, spanning two robots (π0) and π0.5, multiple task types, and consistent metrics (SR and the useful CMR). VAP shows large gains on the hardest disambiguation tasks (e.g., CMR 10.5→89.2 on pen holder; SR 0→71.3 on WidowX shaver).

Baselines are treated unusually fairly: the token-learning (Soft Prompt) baseline is built carefully with oracle hard negatives drawn from the deployment distribution and >95% recognition accuracy, and the appendix provides a principled defense of the VLM→VLA token transfer proxy (Table 8 embedding-space analysis) plus attention-heatmap diagnostics explaining why token learning fails at control.

Honest and informative limitations/error analysis: Table 6/9 disentangles grounding failures from manipulation failures, cross-view inconsistency is identified as the dominant multi-view failure mode, and the conclusion and Appendix E scope the contribution to single-object, short-horizon tabletop tasks without overclaiming.
Runtime overhead is measured (0.26s init, ~10% per-step overhead), addressing a practical deployment concern.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: VAP is a pipeline composition of existing off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM2) plus visual prompting ideas already explored in robotics (RoboGround, MOKA, PIVOT). The genuinely new element is reference-image-based instance retrieval feeding pixel-space prompts, which is somewhat incremental; the 'top-down attention' cognitive framing is largely rhetorical.

Some results show modest margins where it matters: on Task 2 (bottle) VAP's SR 60.6/58.2 is essentially on par with Hard Prompt (58.8/54.2), and on Personalized-VLABench the cup task gain over Soft Prompt is ~6 points. Real-world absolute success rates (56.2% avg pick-and-place) remain moderate, indicating the pipeline does not fully solve instance-conditioned control.

Evaluation is restricted to a single backbone family (π0/π0.5); it is unclear how VAP transfers to other VLAs with different vision encoders or instruction formats, which weakens the generality claim that this is a generic 'perceptual adapter' for frozen VLAs.

Scenarios are relatively easy for the grounding side: only 2 same-category distractors per episode, single personal object, tabletop, short-horizon tasks. The core claim (instance-level disambiguation) would be more convincing with denser distractor clutter, multiple personal objects, or longer horizons; the authors acknowledge this only partially.

Reproducibility is not fully assured: while experimental details are extensive (Appendix A, prompts in A.3), the paper does not state that code, benchmark assets, or 3D models will be released, which is significant given the contribution's weight on two new benchmarks.

The Soft Prompt baseline is necessarily a proxy (tokens learned in PaliGemma and transferred), and although Appendix B defends it well, a direct comparison against an image-conditioning VLM planner that can see the reference images at inference (e.g., a PIVOT-style loop) is missing; such a baseline would more directly test whether pixel-space prompting is superior to VLM-based disambiguation with references.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly formulated problem: personalized ('my cup') manipulation among same-category distractors is a real gap in current VLA evaluations, and the paper articulates why language-only disambiguation is brittle.

Substantial and multi-faceted evaluation: two newly constructed simulation benchmarks (Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench) plus a real-world SO-101 setup spanning selection and pick-and-place tasks, with consistent gains over generic, hard-prompt, and token-learning baselines (e.g., Table 2: SR 60.3% vs 8.5% baseline).

Unusually rigorous treatment of the strongest baseline: the Soft Prompt (token learning) baseline is strengthened with oracle hard negatives drawn from the actual test-time distractors, achieving >95% recognition accuracy, and the paper openly acknowledges this is a leakage-like setting favorable to the baseline.

Good analysis beyond headline numbers: failure-mode taxonomy (Table 6/9), attention heatmaps explaining why token learning fails in closed loop (Appendix B.3), sensitivity to reference count K, opacity/mask-vs-box ablations, and runtime analysis showing only 0.02 s/step overhead.

Honest limitations discussion: multi-view inconsistency is identified as a dominant failure mode (~50-59% of failures in multi-view settings), and the appendix offers a serious formal treatment of cross-view association even though it is left unimplemented.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: VAP is essentially a pipeline of off-the-shelf components (Grounding DINO for proposals, DINOv2 embeddings for matching, SAM2 for tracking, a fixed-color tint overlay, and a string-match instruction rewrite 'my X' -> 'the red X'). Mark/box-based visual prompting for manipulation and reference-image conditioning already exist (Moka, PIVOT, RoboGround, PIN, MEMENTO); the contribution is a recombination applied to instance disambiguation rather than a new method or insight.

The grounding module arguably does all the intellectual work, making the VLA component nearly vacuous: once only the target is tinted a distinctive color and the instruction rewritten to 'the red cup', the policy faces a trivially disambiguated single-target task. The paper does not clearly separate the contribution of instance matching from the contribution of simply recoloring/highlighting one object; a 'highlight a random same-category object' or 'highlight a non-target object' control would test whether the gains reflect personalization at all.

Benchmarks are small and task diversity is thin: only 2 personal categories on Google Robot, 4 on WidowX, 5 on VLABench, and 8 real categories with just 3 physical instances each (1 target + 2 distractors). Claims of 'instance-level generalization' rest on a small object set, and no statistical significance or variance is reported for the simulation results.

Fixed-color highlighting and rewriting introduce unstated brittleness: conflicts between the tint color and the object's true color, red distractors in the scene, or overlapping highlight and grasp-relevant appearance cues are never analyzed, even though the method's central mechanism is precisely this overlay.

The claimed framing as 'input-side adapter'/'visual attentive prompting' oversells what is a detection-then-recolor cascade; failures dominated by Case 3 (correct prompt but failed manipulation, 78-87% of single-view failures) indicate the approach largely reduces to the VLA's existing competence, and the method contributes little to actual control.

Reproducibility is uncertain: no explicit statement that code or the new benchmarks will be released; evaluation pipelines involve numerous tuned choices (voting rule, opacity, rewrite templates, fallback behaviors) whose implementations would be difficult to reconstruct.

Some writing/claims are inflated relative to evidence, e.g., describing the method as bridging 'semantic understanding and instance-level control' when, per the failure analysis, roughly half or more of VAP's remaining failures are plain manipulation failures, and cross-view consistency-a core requirement for the multi-view benchmarks-is acknowledged to be unsolved.
